newsitem.title: USA: Prices boost U.S. soybean acres to highest in 15 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Prices boost U.S. soybean acres to highest in 15 yrs.

text.p: Good weather, favourable prices and fewer farm programme restrictions encouraged U.S. farmers to plant the most acres of soybeans this year since 1982, the U.S. Agriculture Department said on Monday.

Based on its annual survey of farmers during the first two weeks of June, the department pegged soybean plantings at 70.9 million acres, up 10 percent from 1996 and well above its March estimate of 68.8 million.

The new acreage estimate sent soybean prices sharply lower on the Chicago Board of Trade. As of midday, the November soybean contract -- which reflects prices farmers will receive at harvest -- was down 30 cents per bushel, the maximum price decline allowed for the day.
Most analysts had expected the Agriculture Department to lower its estimate of soybean plantings based on weather that seemed to favour corn instead.

But in another surprise, the department pegged corn plantings at just 80.2 million acres. That was the largest since 1985, but well below the March forecast of 81.4 million acres and the average industry estimate of 81.8 million.
Peter Riley, a feed grains analyst in the department's Economic Research Service, attributed the change in corn and soybean acreage estimates to two factors.

Soybean prices since the March estimates, which were also based on a survey of farmers, have been "extremely attractive," he said. Changes made last year to U.S. farm programmes have made it much easier for farmers to alter spring planting plans in response to changing market conditions, he noted.
"If anything can be gleaned (from Monday's report) it's that 'Freedom to Farm' does work," said Dick Loewy, president of AgResource Inc., using the popular nickname for the landmark 1996 farm bill.
"We were mesmerised this spring by early plantings but we should have seen this coming," Loewy said.

Under the 1996 farm bill, government subsidy payments are no longer tied to particular crops. As a result, farmers now have more freedom to switch from one crop to another without losing government payments.
This spring, "farmers really responded to the market incentives and planted (soybeans) big time," Riley said.
However, U.S. soybean supplies will remain tight until at least the fall harvest because of relatively small crops over the past two years.

In its quarterly Grain Stocks report, also released Monday, the Agriculture Department pegged U.S. soybean stocks on June 1 at just 499 million bushels, down 20 percent from last year and the lowest since 1989.
The tight supplies raise the stakes for the 1997 soybean crop -- which so far appears to in good shape -- and should keep traders on edge.
"Until the new crop comes in, there's going to be a little apprehension" over final yields and acreage, the department's Riley said.
